title: Building an offer that justifies a higher rate for Healthcare cleaning (aged care, medical, dental, NDIS)
audience: Owners and supervisors of healthcare cleaning businesses (aged care, medical, dental and NDIS-funded settings) who write offers for facility managers and practice managers.
learningOutcomes: Write a cleaning offer for a care or clinical setting with a clear outcome, time frame and conditions, without promising clinical results
Identify the friction and risk the facility carries, including access, timing and sign-off, and reduce them
Price the offer on the facility's scope and risk, and check the price against your own cost and time

instruction.heading: A bad offer versus a good offer for a facility
instruction.body: 'We clean your clinic' is a service. 'We clean the treatment rooms, waiting area and high-touch surfaces named on your written schedule, sign the checklist at each visit, and re-clean any listed area that fails the checklist at no charge' is an offer. A practice manager buys a result she can check against her own schedule and records. She does not buy a promise of infection control, which the facility's clinical and infection-control staff decide.

instruction.heading: The five parts of an offer for a facility
instruction.body: A clear outcome, written as the areas and tasks named in the facility's cleaning schedule; a defined time frame, such as an after-hours window the site allows; what the facility must provide, such as access, keys, a sign-off contact and any site induction it requires; the certainty you provide, such as a signed checklist and a visit log; and the risk you carry, such as a re-clean commitment you can keep. Put the scope and exclusions in writing. Clinical waste handling, sharps, instrument work and clinical duties are not part of a cleaning offer unless the facility's procedure sets them, and the local rule decides who is responsible for waste. A written quote can become binding once it is accepted (business.gov.au, 1 August 2025).

instruction.heading: Reducing friction for the facility
instruction.body: Facility staff have limited time and strict routines. Make booking, induction, access and sign-off simple. Agree one contact who signs the checklist. Confirm that cleaning does not clash with care routines, clinic sessions or procedures, and write the agreed window into the schedule. Fewer decisions for the facility usually supports a higher price, because the facility pays for reliability and fewer disruptions.

instruction.heading: Guarantees, claims and a fix-first promise
instruction.body: A written workmanship warranty is an optional promise that sits on top of the statutory consumer guarantees and cannot remove them, and a 'no refunds' line does not override a customer's rights for services (business.gov.au, 27 May 2025). A fix-first promise, where you re-clean a failed area at no charge, fits the expectation that a business gets a reasonable chance to fix a minor fault free of charge (Consumer Victoria, 13 October 2023); that page does not set a fix-window length. Do not claim infection-free, sterile or pathogen-free results. The research for this course has no source for clinical result claims, so check current ACCC guidance and the facility's own rules before you publish any measurable claim.

instruction.heading: Pricing on value, with GST shown
instruction.body: Price from the outcome, the certainty and the risk, then check the price against your cost and time. The research for this course has no healthcare price source, so the rate must come from your own costs and the facility's scope. Misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026), and the quote should show one clear total with a statement of whether GST is included (WA Consumer Protection, 4 September 2026). A stepped offer can help a facility choose: a routine clean, a routine clean with high-touch and spill response, or a full scheduled clean. Each higher level should add something the facility can see on its checklist (Jobber Academy, May 2021, updated 8 October 2024). Any extra work outside the schedule is priced in writing before it starts. Business Queensland suggests charging added costs at cost plus 15 per cent; that is one source's suggestion, not a healthcare benchmark.

procedure: Write the outcome as the areas and tasks named in the facility's cleaning schedule, in one sentence a practice manager would repeat.
Set a visit window the facility allows, and record how often you have met similar windows.
List what the facility must provide, including access, induction and a sign-off contact, and reduce each step.
Add one certainty element, such as a signed checklist and a visit log.
Decide the re-clean commitment and check that you can deliver it within your own capacity.
Price from scope and risk, check the rate against cost and time, then show the total with its GST status.

workedExamples.situation: A dental practice's current cleaner is cheaper, but the practice manager cannot tell which rooms are covered or when the work happens around appointments. She asks for a new quote covering after-hours cleaning of the treatment rooms and the waiting area.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the offer name, what should it leave out, and how should it be priced?
workedExamples.reasoning: The offer names the treatment rooms and waiting area from the practice's written schedule, the after-hours window agreed with the practice, the checklist the practice signs at each visit, and a re-clean of any listed area that fails. It leaves out clinical waste handling, sharps and instrument work, and says so in writing. Victorian EPA guidance from 2009 (status unverified) says the generator of clinical waste is responsible, so the quote asks the practice to confirm who handles waste under its local rule. The checklist names the frequently touched surfaces, which the NHMRC guidelines (2019 edition as read; check the current version) say should be cleaned with detergent at least daily, and routine cleaning runs from high to low and from clean to dirty (NSW Health ECSOP Module 3, October 2024). PPE and disinfectant choices follow the local rule, because the research has no source for them. The price is set from your own cost per hour and the agreed scope, not from a healthcare rate, because the research found no healthcare price source. The total and its GST status are shown. No price figure is given in this example.

commonErrors.error: Promising an infection-control result the cleaner cannot control
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the cleaning you deliver against the facility's schedule and checklist, and leave infection-control outcomes to the facility's own staff.

commonErrors.error: Quoting without exclusions for waste, sharps or instrument work
commonErrors.prevention: List what is excluded, and confirm in writing who handles waste under the local rule.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business guidance only. Aged care, medical, dental and NDIS-funded facilities may set their own contract, induction and infection-control terms, and state rules apply. This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority, and does not decide any clinical or infection-control question.

qualityStandard: Every offer to a facility names the areas, visit window, checklist and exclusions, and is checked against cost and time.
documentationEvidence: Written offer with scope, exclusions, visit window and GST status; the facility's signed checklist; and the cost and time check used to set the price.
summary: A healthcare offer promises a checkable result against the facility's own schedule, with a time frame, certainty and a fair re-clean commitment.
Set the price from scope and risk, not from a healthcare rate the research did not find, and state the total and GST status.
